passage:
I'm Pema, and my son is ten months old. Last week, at three in the morning, rocking him in the dark, I suddenly thought of my mother.

Urmila, my Amala, raised me alone in Kalimpong. She sold momos from a cart all evening and came home after I was asleep. As a child I hated that cart. I remember eating cold rice alone and crying for her, and some of that anger is still in me.

But now I'm a mother too, with a husband, a washing machine and a salary, and I'm still exhausted. How did she do it with nothing? I cried, rocking my son, for the girl I was and for the woman she was.

I called her in the morning and just said, "Amala, thank you. I didn't know." She laughed and said, "Now you know."

I'm still going to do some things differently. I won't leave my son to eat alone. But I understand her now.

qa.q: What did Pema's mother sell from a cart?
qa.a: She sold momos from a cart all evening.

qa.q: What did Pema feel, rocking the baby at three in the morning?
qa.a: Pema felt a new tenderness for her mother, mixed with old anger and sadness for the lonely child she had been.

qa.q: How does Pema hold both respect and change?
qa.a: She thanks her mother and understands her struggle, while still naming that she won't leave her son to eat alone.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt hearing her daughter's thanks?
qa.a: Urmila probably felt moved and quietly vindicated, laughing and saying, "Now you know."

grounding: A first-person account shows a new mother who now sees how hard her own mother had it, feeling tenderness and some anger, deepening respect while naming what she will do differently.

passage:
Fathers' group note, session five, community centre, Pune.

Abhinav, 26, spoke for the first time today. His daughter is four months old. He said that walking her at night, he has started thinking about his own father, who drove a tempo sixteen hours a day and came home short-tempered. "I used to hate him for shouting. Now I'm this tired after one baby, and he had four of us."

His voice broke. He said he feels tenderness for his father for the first time and, in the same breath, still angry about the shouting.

Asif, another father, said, "You can understand him and still not become him." Abhinav nodded hard.

I asked him to write two lists: what he now respects in his father, and what he will do differently. He wrote four things on the first list. On the second, one line: "I will not shout at my children to let out my tiredness." He plans to call his father this weekend.

qa.q: How many hours a day did Abhinav's father drive the tempo?
qa.a: He drove a tempo sixteen hours a day.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Abhinav describe about his father?
qa.a: Abhinav felt tenderness for his father for the first time, alongside lingering anger about the shouting.

qa.q: How did the group leader help Abhinav use this new understanding?
qa.a: By asking him to write what he respects in his father and what he will do differently, so respect grows without excusing the shouting.

qa.q: What did Asif offer from his own view as a father?
qa.a: Asif offered the idea that Abhinav can understand his father and still choose not to become him.

grounding: A group leader's note shows a new father who begins to see how hard his own father had it, feeling tenderness and anger, deepening respect while naming what he will do differently.

passage:
You want the honest version? Fine. I'm Pooja, and before my daughter, I was the architect who stayed till midnight because the model wasn't perfect. I loved it. The deadlines, the site visits in boots.

Now I'm home with a one-year-old and I know every song in the nursery rhyme channel. Some afternoons, watching her nap, I'd feel this ache for my old life, and then immediately think, What kind of mother misses anything? The guilt was worse than the ache.

A friend said something that stuck: "You can grieve your old self and still love your new life. Both are true."

So I asked Uday for Saturday mornings. Three hours, just mine. The first Saturday, I sat in a café with a sketchbook and cried a bit. The second, I drew a small library for our colony. It's terrible. It's mine.

I'm a mother who designs buildings. Or will again. Both.

qa.q: What did Pooja draw on the second Saturday?
qa.a: She drew a small library for their colony.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel watching her daughter nap?
qa.a: Pooja felt an ache for her old life and then guilt for missing it, and the guilt was worse than the ache.

qa.q: What helped Pooja make room for her old self?
qa.a: Asking Uday for three hours every Saturday morning and using them to sketch, without shame.

qa.q: How might Uday see Pooja's Saturday mornings?
qa.a: Uday may see them as a fair and good thing, since they help Pooja feel like herself again.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young mother who misses her old career pace and then feels guilty, who makes time for herself and sees her new identity including the old one.

passage:
Before. It was a Thursday in November. Tejas's bass guitar had stood in the corner, zipped in its case, for seven months, since Neel was born. Harsha texted: "Gig on Saturday, we need you." Tejas typed "can't, baby stuff" and then sat looking at the case, missing it so much his throat hurt. Then he felt ashamed. He had a son now. What kind of father pined for a guitar?

During. On Sunday he told his wife. "I miss playing. And I feel terrible for missing it." She laughed, not unkindly. "I miss my running club. Missing things doesn't mean we love him less." They agreed: Tuesday nights for him, Thursday mornings for her.

After. The next month, at a small café, Tejas played two songs with Harsha's band. He came home at eleven, kissed Neel's sleeping head, and felt, for the first time in months, like the whole of himself.

qa.q: How long had the bass guitar stood in its case?
qa.a: It had stood in its case for seven months.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as he looked at the guitar case on Thursday?
qa.a: Tejas felt a painful longing to play and then shame for missing it as a new father.

qa.q: What arrangement helped Tejas and his wife?
qa.a: They each took a regular slot for themselves, Tuesday nights for him and Thursday mornings for her, without guilt.

qa.q: How does Tejas's wife see his missing music?
qa.a: She sees it as normal, missing things herself, and not as a sign he loves their son less.

grounding: The story shows a new father who misses his old life and feels guilty, then makes time for himself without shame and finds that his new identity can include the old one.

passage:
Hrithik, puttar, you think you're helping Simran by washing the bottles. Listen to your Jasleen biji first.

When your chacha was born, your dadaji thought he was a very modern man. He changed a nappy on Sundays. He would say, "Just tell me what to do." But I was the one who knew when the milk powder ran out, when the vaccination was due, which neighbour's girl could babysit. All of it in my head. Nobody saw it. I felt like a ghost in my own home, and I was angry, all the time.

One night I didn't cry or shout. I sat down with a notebook and wrote every single job, even the small ones. Forty-two things. I gave it to him. "Pick half. Not to help me. To own."

He read it twice. He took the vaccinations, the shopping list and the nights on Fridays. It was the beginning of a real partnership.

qa.q: How many jobs did Jasleen write in the notebook?
qa.a: She wrote forty-two jobs.

qa.q: How did young Jasleen feel carrying all the unseen work?
qa.a: She felt invisible, like a ghost in her own home, and angry all the time.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jasleen's story?
qa.a: Writing every task in a notebook and asking her husband to pick half to own, not just help with.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's husband have felt reading the list?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a little ashamed, having not seen how much she carried, and he took real tasks.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young mother whose partner did not see her unseen work with the baby, who named the tasks in a list and asked for ownership rather than help.

passage:
The paediatrician's appointment was at nine, Mitali had a board meeting at nine-thirty, and Varun found out at eight-fifteen that the diaper bag was empty. Nobody had refilled it. Nobody but him ever did.

He packed it one-handed, the baby on his hip, and something hot rose in his chest. He had quit his office job to stay home. Mitali called it "helping out" when she gave the baby a bath. She had no idea who remembered the vaccinations, the rash cream, the new shoe size.

That night he didn't sulk. He wrote a list on the fridge: every task, from doctor visits to sterilising bottles. "I don't want help," he said. "I want you to own some of these. Completely." Mitali read the list slowly. "I really didn't see half of this." She picked the doctor visits and the weekend shopping.

Next door, Chaitanya had seen the list through the window. "Can I copy that?" he asked.

qa.q: What did Varun find out at eight-fifteen?
qa.a: He found out the diaper bag was empty.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he packed the bag one-handed?
qa.a: Varun felt angry and invisible, with something hot rising in his chest because nobody saw the work he did.

qa.q: How did Varun ask for change without becoming a martyr?
qa.a: He wrote every task on a list and asked Mitali to fully own some of them, instead of sulking or doing it all silently.

qa.q: How did Mitali see the list?
qa.a: Mitali was surprised and honest, admitting she hadn't seen half of the work.

grounding: The story shows a stay-at-home father whose wife does not see the unseen work with the baby, who names tasks in a list and asks for equal ownership rather than help.

passage:
The power had gone out at eleven, the inverter had died at one, and baby Myra had a slight fever. Anjali sat in the dark flat fanning her with a newspaper, and the only light was her phone, where her cousin's perfect baby was smiling in a spotless nursery.

No fever there, Anjali thought. No mess. No mother crying at two a.m. She felt she was failing at every single thing.

Pradeep woke, found her there and sat beside her. "What does Dr. Gill always say?"

"Keep her cool, give fluids, call if it keeps going or worries us."

"Are you doing that?"

She was. She had been, all night.

He took the phone gently and put it face down. "That video is two minutes long. This is real. And she's fine because you're here."

At dawn Myra's forehead was cooler. They kept to her usual routine: feed, bath, nap. Anjali called the clinic anyway, and the nurse said she was doing everything right.

qa.q: When did the inverter die?
qa.a: The inverter died at one.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling as she watched her cousin's video?
qa.a: Anjali felt inadequate and anxious, as if she was failing at every single thing.

qa.q: What helped Anjali move away from comparison?
qa.a: Pradeep reminded her of the doctor's simple advice, she saw she was already following it, and she trusted their usual routine and the clinic.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see Anjali that night?
qa.a: Pradeep sees her as a loving, capable mother whose presence is what the baby needs.

grounding: The story shows a young mother comparing herself with a relative's online video and feeling never enough, who comes back to simple routines and her doctor's guidance.

passage:
At the family lunch in Rekha's parents' flat in Chembur, everyone had advice for Tanvir. His brother-in-law's son was already potty trained. A cousin's daughter was saying whole sentences at eighteen months. Tanvir's son, two now, had eaten three chapatis, shouted "No!" at an aunt, and fallen asleep under the table.

On the drive home Tanvir said nothing for ten minutes. Then: "We're behind on everything. I'm getting it all wrong."

Rekha looked at him. "Behind whom? He's happy. He sleeps. He laughs at your jokes."

"They all seem so sure."

"They were sure about our wedding food too." Tanvir smiled despite himself.

At home, while Rekha bathed their son, Tanvir looked up the doctor's advice sheet from the last visit. He's growing well, it said; continue the same routines. Tanvir stuck it on the fridge. That night he read the same dinosaur book three times, badly, and his son giggled every time.

qa.q: What had Tanvir's son done at the family lunch?
qa.a: He ate three chapatis, shouted "No!" at an aunt and fell asleep under the table.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on the drive home?
qa.a: Tanvir felt anxious and inadequate, sure they were behind and he was getting everything wrong.

qa.q: What helped Tanvir trust himself again?
qa.a: Rekha's calm questions, and rereading the doctor's sheet that said to continue the same routines.

qa.q: How does Rekha see their son?
qa.a: Rekha sees him as happy and well, not behind anyone, and she is not shaken by relatives' comparisons.

grounding: The passage shows a young father comparing his parenting with relatives and feeling not enough, who comes back to simple routines and his doctor's guidance.

passage:
Zeenat is two, and on Tuesday she poured her water on the floor nine times. I counted. I'm Sahil, her father, and I want to tell you about the ninth time, because that's when I nearly lost it.

I had wiped it up eight times. I had said "No" eight times. On the ninth she looked right at me and tipped the cup, slowly, and I felt my face go hot. I raised my voice. "Zeenat!" Loud. She froze, lip shaking.

I put her in her high chair, safe, and walked to the kitchen door. I breathed out, counted to ten, and looked at the tap until my hands stopped shaking. I told myself: she's two. She's learning what water does. She's not trying to break me.

Then I went back and sat low beside her. Quieter. "Water stays in the cup. You can pour it in the bath." That evening, in the bath, she poured for twenty minutes, delighted.

qa.q: How many times did Zeenat pour her water on the floor?
qa.a: She poured it nine times.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel on the ninth pour?
qa.a: Sahil felt his patience snap, his face hot with anger.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Putting Zeenat somewhere safe and stepping away for a minute let Sahil calm down, then come back quietly and give her a place where pouring was allowed.

qa.q: What was the raised voice like for Zeenat?
qa.a: It frightened her, since she froze and her lip shook.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young father whose toddler tests him until his patience thins, who steps away safely, calms down and remembers the child is learning.

passage:
Monday. At bedtime Sonali, three, got out of bed eleven times: water, a toy, a tummy ache, "one more hug". By the eleventh, Shalini was shouting down the corridor, "Go to SLEEP!" Sonali sobbed herself to sleep, and Shalini sat in the kitchen feeling awful.

Wednesday. Shalini's patience was thin again by the sixth trip. This time, before her voice rose, she stopped in the corridor, put one hand on the wall, and breathed out three times. She told herself: she's three, she's testing, not plotting. Then she knelt down. "It's sleep time. I'll check on you in five minutes." Her voice came out low.

The following Monday. Shalini had made a picture chart with Sonali: bath, story, water, one hug, sleep. Sonali still got up twice, just to check the chart. The third time, she fell asleep holding it. Shalini stood in the doorway, tired, and a little proud of both of them.

qa.q: How many times did Sonali get out of bed on Monday?
qa.a: She got out of bed eleven times.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel sitting in the kitchen on Monday night?
qa.a: Shalini felt awful and guilty after shouting at Sonali.

qa.q: What small step helped Shalini on Wednesday?
qa.a: Pausing with a hand on the wall and breathing before her voice rose, then kneeling and speaking low.

qa.q: How might the picture chart feel for Sonali?
qa.a: The chart gives Sonali a sense of safety and control, knowing what comes next.

grounding: The story shows a young mother whose toddler tests her at bedtime until her patience thins, who learns over days to pause, breathe and lower her voice.

passage:
I'm Raghav, and I still remember the cold of the frozen foods aisle. Sachin, three, lay flat on the supermarket floor, kicking and screaming because I had put back the chocolate eggs.

"Papa, I HATE you!"

People stared. An old man tutted. A teenager filmed with his phone. I felt my face burn, and under the embarrassment a hot fury: at Sachin, at the old man, at myself.

I wanted to drag him out by the arm. Instead I crouched, moved the trolley so no one would trip on him, and said nothing except, "I'm here. You're safe." I waited. It felt like an hour. It was probably four minutes.

When he finally sat up, sweaty and hiccuping, I carried him out and we sat in the car.

Later, at bedtime, he whispered, "Sorry, Papa." I said, "I was angry too. We both calmed down. That's good." He fell asleep holding my finger.

qa.q: What had Raghav put back that started the tantrum?
qa.a: He had put back the chocolate eggs.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as people stared?
qa.a: Raghav felt embarrassed, his face burning, and underneath that a hot fury at Sachin, the old man and himself.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's choices kept things safe and calm?
qa.a: He crouched, moved the trolley so no one tripped, stayed near and quiet, waited it out, and talked about it gently at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt once the tantrum ended?
qa.a: Sachin was likely worn out and a little sorry, whispering an apology at bedtime.

grounding: A first-person account shows a father whose toddler screams at him in public, feeling embarrassed and furious, who stays calm, keeps the child safe, waits it out and reconnects later.

passage:
Preschool note, Friday pickup.

Afreen (3) refused to leave the sandpit at pickup time and, when her mother Aditi lifted her, screamed and hit at her face. Several parents at the gate turned to look. Aditi's cheeks went red and her jaw tightened. I heard her say, through her teeth, "Stop it right now," and then she stopped herself.

She put Afreen down on the soft mat, knelt next to her, and said quietly, "I won't let you hit. I'll wait here." She kept a hand near her so she couldn't run to the road. It took about five minutes.

Afterwards Aditi told me she felt humiliated and very angry, and ashamed that she had nearly shouted. I told her she had kept Afreen safe and stayed steady, which is what matters.

On Monday Afreen brought me a drawing "for Mummy and me". Aditi said they had talked about the sandpit at home and made up with a hug.

qa.q: Where did Afreen refuse to leave?
qa.a: She refused to leave the sandpit at pickup time.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel as the parents at the gate looked on?
qa.a: Aditi felt humiliated and very angry, her cheeks red and jaw tight, and later ashamed that she nearly shouted.

qa.q: What did Aditi do that kept Afreen safe?
qa.a: She put her down on the soft mat, knelt beside her, stopped the hitting calmly, kept her from running to the road, and waited.

qa.q: How might Afreen have experienced her mother's calm response?
qa.a: Afreen likely felt held and safe even in her anger, and later showed it with a drawing for her mother.

grounding: A preschool teacher's note shows a young mother whose child has a public tantrum, feeling embarrassed and furious, who stays calm, keeps the child safe and repairs later.

passage:
Nitin kept the accounts for half the shops on the main road of Barwani, and on Friday evening he had forty pages to finish. Mehak, five, wanted to help. She dipped his fountain pen into the ink and dragged it across the page.

"Mehak! What have you DONE?" His shout rattled the window. She dropped the pen and ran behind the curtain.

Nitin sat very still. His heart was pounding, and then, slowly, it turned into a heavy, sick feeling. She had only wanted to help.

His first thought was to take her to the sweet shop and buy her anything she wanted. He didn't. He went to the curtain and knelt.

"Mehak, I shouted very loudly. I was scared about my work, but shouting was wrong. I'm sorry." She peeked out. He showed her a scrap page. "Let's draw with ink here, together."

They drew a crooked elephant. Then he finished the accounts, late.

qa.q: What did Mehak do with the fountain pen?
qa.a: She dipped it in the ink and dragged it across his page.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after he shouted?
qa.a: Nitin felt a heavy, sick guilt once his pounding heart settled, knowing she had only wanted to help.

qa.q: Why was Nitin's apology better than a trip to the sweet shop?
qa.a: A simple apology that named what happened, followed by drawing together, repaired the bond without buying off the guilt.

qa.q: What was the shout like for Mehak?
qa.a: It frightened her, and she ran to hide behind the curtain.

grounding: The passage shows a young father who snaps at his child and feels awful, apologising simply, naming what happened and reconnecting instead of overindulging.

passage:
In their small apartment in Buenos Aires, Alejandro was on a work call when Yosef, four, crashed his toy truck into the laptop for the third time. "Enough!" Alejandro barked, and grabbed the truck. Yosef's face crumpled and he ran to his room.

Alejandro finished the call with half his mind. Afterward he sat on the sofa feeling awful. His own father had shouted like that, and he had promised himself never.

He found Yosef under the blanket. "Can I come in?" A small nod.

"I shouted at you and took your truck. I was stressed about work. That wasn't fair, and I'm sorry."

Yosef sniffed. "You were scary."

"I know. Next time I'll say, 'Papa needs five minutes,' before I get angry."

He gave the truck back. They built a ramp out of books, and when the next call came, Yosef whispered, "Papa needs five minutes," and pushed his truck to the other room.

qa.q: How old was Yosef?
qa.a: Yosef was four.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling on the sofa after the call?
qa.a: Alejandro felt awful and guilty, especially because he had promised himself never to shout like his own father.

qa.q: What made Alejandro's repair work?
qa.a: He apologised simply, named what he did and why it was unfair, offered a plan for next time, and reconnected through play.

qa.q: How did Yosef experience his father's shout?
qa.a: Yosef found it scary, crumpling and running to hide under his blanket.

grounding: The passage shows a young father who snaps at his child and feels awful, who apologises simply, names what happened and reconnects.

passage:
In Kalimpong the lanes run steeply downhill, and Pema had never let four-year-old Karma walk even to the corner shop's step alone. She held his hand, his collar, sometimes both.

Nazia from next door watched her one afternoon. Nazia's own boys were racing tyres down the lane. "Pema, he's looking at them like a prisoner."

Pema laughed, then didn't. She saw it: Karma standing stiff beside her, not asking to play anymore. Her worry had become his.

The next day she tried something small. "You can walk to the Lepcha aunty's shop step by yourself. I'll watch from here." Twenty metres, no road to cross. Karma looked at her as if she had handed him a sword.

He went, slowly, turning back twice. He came back holding a toffee and grinning.

Pema's stomach had been in knots the whole time. She didn't say that. She said, "You did it," and let go of his collar.

qa.q: How old was Karma?
qa.a: Karma was four.

qa.q: What did Pema feel while Karma walked to the shop step?
qa.a: Pema felt anxious, her stomach in knots, though she kept it to herself.

qa.q: What small risk did Pema allow, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She let Karma walk twenty metres alone with no road to cross while she watched, so he could build courage without real danger.

qa.q: How did Karma seem to feel before and after the walk?
qa.a: Before, he seemed held back and stiff; after, he was proud and grinning with his toffee.

grounding: The passage shows an anxious parent who sees her worry holding her child back and consciously allows a small, safe risk so he can learn courage.

passage:
In the park in Kadıköy, Jin sat on the edge of the bench, ready to jump. Zeynep, five, wanted to climb the tall rope net. Every time she reached the second row, Jin called out, "Careful! Come down a bit!" and she came down.

After the fourth time she stopped trying and sat in the sand, poking it with a stick.

Jin felt a jolt. He knew that look. It was his own, from childhood, when his mother wouldn't let him ride a bike.

He walked over and crouched. "Zeynep, try again. I'll stand at the bottom and I won't say anything."

She looked suspicious. Then she climbed. Second row, third row, fourth. Jin's hands were clenched in his pockets. At the fifth row she shouted, "Baba, look how high!"

"I see you," he called, and meant it, and his voice only shook a little.

qa.q: Which park were Jin and Zeynep in?
qa.a: They were in the park in Kadıköy.

qa.q: What did Jin feel when Zeynep sat poking the sand?
qa.a: Jin felt a jolt of recognition and guilt, seeing his own childhood disappointment in her face.

qa.q: What did Jin change, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He stood at the bottom and stayed quiet, letting her try a safe climb, so his fear didn't become hers.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel after Jin let her climb?
qa.a: Zeynep felt proud and thrilled, shouting for him to look how high she was.

grounding: The passage shows a parent whose own worry is holding his child back, who consciously allows a small risk so she learns courage and his fear does not become hers.

passage:
Tarun's cousin's wedding was in two days, the whole family would be there, and Tarun had spent the evening trying to get his son Vivaan, four, to read the word "cat".

"Your cousin Ruhi reads whole books," he snapped. "Try harder." Vivaan's lip trembled and he pushed the book away.

Nazia came in from the kitchen. "What are you doing?"

"Everyone will ask. Ruhi's reading, he isn't. I'm worried something's wrong."

Nazia sat down. "If you're truly worried, we ask his teacher, or the doctor. Not him, at nine at night, two days before a wedding."

Tarun looked at Vivaan, who was drawing a very detailed truck on the back of the book. He felt ashamed of the word "harder".

"Sorry, champ. That truck's brilliant."

The next morning Tarun emailed Vivaan's teacher. Her reply came quickly: he was doing fine, just loved drawing more than letters for now.

qa.q: What word was Tarun trying to get Vivaan to read?
qa.a: He was trying to get him to read the word "cat".

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he compared Vivaan with Ruhi?
qa.a: Tarun felt anxious that something was wrong and that relatives would judge, which made him snap.

qa.q: What did Nazia suggest, and why was it better?
qa.a: She suggested asking the teacher or doctor if truly worried, rather than pushing and shaming Vivaan late at night.

qa.q: How did Vivaan experience his father's comparison?
qa.a: It hurt him; his lip trembled and he pushed the book away.

grounding: The story shows a young father anxious because his child is slower than a cousin, who stops shaming by comparison and asks a professional instead.

passage:
Lalremsiami's son Mawia was two and barely said ten words. Downstairs in their Delhi apartment block, Rajni's girl, the same age, chatted about aeroplanes and the rain. Every evening in the building's garden, Lalremsiami listened and felt her chest tighten.

"Mawia, say aeroplane," she urged one evening, in front of everyone. "Look, Rajni aunty's daughter can." Mawia looked at the ground and walked away to the swings.

That night she couldn't sleep. The comparing wasn't helping him. It was just making him feel small in front of people.

She booked an appointment with his paediatrician. The doctor asked questions, watched Mawia stack blocks and point at a picture of a dog, and said children talk at different paces. "Keep reading and talking to him. We'll check again at his next visit, and come sooner if you're worried."

In the garden the next evening, Lalremsiami didn't compare. She just pushed the swing and named everything they saw.

qa.q: How many words did Mawia say?
qa.a: He barely said ten words.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel listening to Rajni's daughter chatting?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt anxious, her chest tightening as she compared the two children.

qa.q: What steps did Lalremsiami take instead of comparing?
qa.a: She saw a paediatrician about her worry, followed the advice to keep reading and talking, and stopped comparing Mawia in public.

qa.q: How might Mawia have felt when compared in front of everyone?
qa.a: Mawia probably felt small and embarrassed, looking at the ground and walking away.

grounding: The passage shows a young mother anxious because her child talks later than a neighbour's, who consults a professional and stops shaming him with comparisons.

passage:
I'm Tenzin, and when my daughter Dolkar came second in the school drawing contest, I wanted to put her picture on the wall of every tea shop in Darjeeling.

I'll be honest. I wanted to be a painter once. My father said it wasn't a job, so I became an accountant. When Dolkar started drawing, something old woke up in me. I bought her expensive pencils. I corrected her shading. I told Sudha she should do extra classes on Sundays.

Then, at the prize ceremony, Dolkar whispered, "Papa, are you happy with me or with the picture?"

That stopped me.

On the walk home I told her what I really admired: that she drew the tea pickers for three weeks and didn't give up when the hands looked wrong. That she helped her friend with his colours.

Sudha squeezed my arm. No Sunday classes. Dolkar draws when she wants to. I'm proud of her. Not of my old dream.

qa.q: What prize did Dolkar win in the drawing contest?
qa.a: She came second in the school drawing contest.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Dolkar asked her question at the ceremony?

Junior football coach's note, Saturday.

Bhupen (6) scored his first goal today. His father Jagdish ran onto the edge of the pitch shouting, and filmed the rest of the match on his phone, calling out, "Shoot! Shoot every time!" Afterwards he told me, very excited, that he had played for his district as a boy and had to stop when his father fell ill, and that Bhupen "will go further".

Bhupen, meanwhile, was holding his water bottle and looking at his dad, not smiling. He told me later that he likes passing to his friend Kunal.

I took Jagdish aside and said it was clear how proud he was. I asked what he had noticed besides the goal. He thought, and said Bhupen had passed well and helped a boy who fell. I suggested saying exactly that to him.

He did, in the car park. Bhupen's face lit up. Jagdish looked moved and a bit surprised.

qa.q: How old was Bhupen when he scored his first goal?
qa.a: Bhupen was six.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he shouted from the edge of the pitch?
qa.a: Jagdish felt thrilled and proud, and his excitement was tied up with his own lost dream of playing.

qa.q: What did the coach suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To praise the passing and kindness Jagdish had noticed, so Bhupen feels valued for his effort and character, not for living out his father's dream.

qa.q: How did Bhupen experience his father's shouting?
qa.a: Bhupen seemed uneasy and not happy, holding his water bottle and not smiling, preferring to pass to his friend.

grounding: A coach's note shows a proud young father tempted to live his own football dream through his son, who is guided to praise effort and character instead.
